featuredContent: This section brings the “ASD research” content from the web to the mobile app. The texts are for informational purposes; they do not replace diagnosis/treatment.

sections.title: Global and National Research (Summary)
sections.description: Topics include intra-brain communication, genetic mechanisms, environmental triggers, subtypes, and early diagnosis.
sections.content:
1) Intra-Brain Communication and Cellular Structure Differences

University of Aberdeen (Scotland - 2025): In a study published in Nature Communications, the Extracellular Matrix (ECM), which is the intercellular support and signaling network in the brain, was mapped. The research showed how autism-associated genes alter the “wiring” instructions in this cellular scaffolding (matrisome) system. This leads to structural speed and bandwidth differences in data transmission between neural regions during the early stages of brain development.

Harvard University (Tan Yang Autism Center - 2025): Focusing on neurotransmitter mechanisms, the center reported at the cellular level that irregularities in synaptic chemical transmission (especially in the serotonin and glutamate balance) trigger sensory sensitivities and repetitive behavior patterns on the spectrum.

2) Genetic Mechanisms, AI, and the Gender Factor

Princeton University & Simons Foundation (USA - 2025): Over 2,500 new risk genes beyond the known 65 were identified using machine learning and AI algorithms.

Baylor College of Medicine (USA - 2025/2026): The “female protective effect” was investigated at the molecular level; it was reported that a more intense and cumulative genetic mutation load is required in girls for similar symptoms to appear compared to boys.

Üsküdar University (Turkey): Findings were published showing that an increase in TNFα levels suppresses the GRID2 gene, and this plays a role in ASD pathogenesis via the glutamate receptor mechanism.

3) Environmental Triggers, Epigenetics, and Misconceptions

UC Davis MIND Institute (USA - 2025/2026): It was reported that exposure to agricultural pesticides, plastic derivatives (PCBs), and heavy metals in infants with genetic susceptibility can trigger epigenetic mechanisms.

Ege University (Turkey - 2026): It was emphasized that the perception that “screen exposure or neglect causes autism” is false; the picture is a genetically based neurodevelopmental process.

4) Discovery of Biological Subtypes (Personalized Medicine)

Princeton University & Simons Foundation (2025): Analyses of clinical and biological data from over 5,000 children with autism revealed that ASD is divided into 4 different biological subtypes; each subtype can show different mechanisms, developmental courses, and treatment responses.

5) Early Diagnosis and Scientific Education Models

University of Toronto (Canada - 2025): Using computer vision and voice analytics, early risk scoring is targeted by monitoring infants' motor movements, crying frequencies, and social orientations.

İstinye University & Hacettepe University (Turkey): It was stated that there is no drug formula to completely eliminate the core symptoms of autism; the approach with proven efficacy is early, intensive, and individualized special education.

sections.title: Technical Details (Princeton • Üsküdar • UC Davis)
sections.description: Features of the 4 biological subtypes, the GRID2/glutamate mechanism, and adulthood-aging findings.
sections.content:
1) Princeton University and Simons Foundation: Clinical Features of the 4 Biological Subtypes

Princeton University divided autism into 4 main biological subtypes by analyzing fMRI, gene sequencing, and clinical behavior data with AI-based clustering algorithms.

Type 1: Social and Communicative Focused Cluster
- Molecular background: Gene variations related to language development and social attachment (e.g., FOXP2 and OXT oxytocin receptor pathways).
- Clinical presentation: Motor skills and general intelligence level may be within typical limits; difficulties in eye contact, social cues, empathy, and synchronization in reciprocal conversation may be seen.

Type 2: Sensory-Motor and Stereotypic Cluster
- Molecular background: Mutations in genes regulating motor planning and sensory integration centers (basal ganglia and thalamus).
- Clinical presentation: Repetitive movements and sensory sensitivities may be prominent.

Type 3: Developmental Delay and Cognitive Impairment Cluster
- Molecular background: Chromosomal copy number variations (CNVs) affecting cortex stratification.
- Clinical presentation: Severe delay in speech, slowness in motor skills, and need for additional support.

Type 4: Broad Spectrum and Medical Comorbidity Cluster
- Molecular background: Pathways affecting the immune/digestive system in addition to the nervous system (e.g., PTEN, TSC).
- Clinical presentation: Epilepsy, sleep disorders, gastrointestinal problems, and chronic neuro-inflammation may accompany.

2) Üsküdar University: GRID2 Gene and Glutamate Mechanism

In the context of the Excitation/Inhibition imbalance:
Systemic Inflammation (TNFα increase) → Suppression of the GRID2 gene → Glutamate receptor defect → Excessive electrical stimulation in the brain (sensory overload)

Role of the GRID2 gene: Encodes the Ionotropic Glutamate Receptor Delta-2 protein in Purkinje cells in the cerebellum.

TNFα triggering: When TNFα rises, GRID2 gene expression can be suppressed.

Neural outcome: Glutamate balance can be disrupted; this can lead to difficulty in filtering sensory information, motor coordination problems, and differences in learning processes.

3) UC Davis MIND Institute: Aging and Adulthood Research

It has been reported that autism is a lifelong neurobiological process; with aging, volume loss may be faster in some areas (especially the prefrontal cortex), and telomere shortening and cellular stress indicators may be higher.

It has been reported that social “masking” strategies in late-diagnosed individuals (especially women) may be associated with autistic burnout, depression, and anxiety in middle/advanced ages.

sections.title: Personalized Model (From Diagnosis to Adulthood)
sections.description: Effects on education/therapy, drug research by subtypes, and early clinical signals.
sections.content:
I) Personalized Education and Therapy Models for the Princeton 4 Subtypes

Type 1 therapy model
- Focus: Peer interaction, social semantics, reading gestures-facial expressions.
- Model: DIR/Floortime and Social Stories.

Type 2 therapy model
- Focus: Sensory integration, thalamic filtering, motor planning.
- Model: Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) and ABA modification.
- Note: Stereotypies are not directly blocked; the underlying sensory need is identified, the nervous system is regulated, and then skill teaching is initiated.

Type 3 therapy model
- Focus: Alternative communication channels and functional life skills.
- Model: PECS and Early Start Denver Model (ESDM).
- Note: Intensive and structured weekly education (e.g., 20–40 hours) can be targeted.

Type 4 therapy model
- Focus: Medical stabilization first, then multidisciplinary support.
- Model: Medical-biologically supported special education.

II) Effect of Üsküdar University's Glutamate Discovery on Drug Research

1. Targeted glutamate regulators: Aims to prevent excessive glutamate accumulation (excitotoxicity).
2. Anti-inflammatory and cytokine-blocking therapies: Agents targeting neuro-inflammation are research candidates.
3. Gene therapies and mRNA technology: Targeted approaches are being investigated for individuals experiencing GRID2 loss of function.

III) Early Clinical Signals in Early Childhood

0–9 months
- Unresponsiveness to name: Hearing the sound but not prioritizing it as a “social stimulus.”
- Delay in social smiling.

9–12 months
- Sensory overreaction or unresponsiveness.
- Deviation in eye tracking: locking onto the finger instead of the pointed object.

12–18 months
- Significant difficulty in imitation skills.
- Fixation on spinning objects/wheels.
- Possibility of babbling/word regression.

sections.title: Practical Tracking of Mechanisms
sections.description: M-CHAT-R/F screening, sensory diet plan, and structuring family involvement.
sections.content:
I) M-CHAT-R/F Screening Tool and Scoring at Home

M-CHAT-R is a 20-question screening tool that determines risk in children aged 16–30 months. It does not diagnose; it measures the risk level.

Critical items (summary)
1. Does your child enjoy being swung, bounced on your knee, etc.? (Normal: Yes)
2. Does your child take an interest in other children? (Normal: Yes)
3. Does your child like climbing on things? (Normal: Yes)
4. Does your child enjoy playing peek-a-boo/hide-and-seek? (Normal: Yes)
5. Does your child ever use his/her index finger to point, to ask for something? (Normal: Yes)
6. Does your child ever use his/her index finger to point, to indicate interest in something? (Normal: Yes)
7. Does your child play properly with small toys (e.g. cars or blocks) without just mouthing, fiddling, or dropping them? (Normal: Yes)
8. Does your child ever bring objects over to you to show you something? (Normal: Yes)
9. Does your child look you in the eye for more than a second or two? (Normal: Yes)
10. Does your child seem oversensitive to noise? (Normal: No)
11. Does your child smile in response to your face or your smile? (Normal: Yes)
12. Does your child respond to his/her name when you call? (Normal: Yes)
13. If you point at a toy across the room, does your child look at it? (Normal: Yes)
14. Does your child walk? (Normal: Yes)
15. Does your child look at things you are looking at? (Normal: Yes)
16. Does your child make unusual finger movements near his/her face? (Normal: No)
17. Does your child try to copy what you do? (Normal: Yes)
18. Have you ever wondered if your child is deaf? (Normal: No)
19. Does your child understand what people say? (Normal: Yes)
20. Does your child sometimes stare at nothing or wander with no purpose? (Normal: No)

Scoring
- Every answer other than “Normal” is 1 point.
- 0–2: Low risk
- 3–7: Medium risk (follow-up interview)
- 8–20: High risk (referral to a specialist)

II) Sensory Diet in the Home Environment

Proprioceptive (deep pressure) activities
- Sandwich game (rhythmic pressure with a cushion)
- Heavy work (pushing a basket, mimicking lifting weights)
- Chewing gum/hard food

Vestibular regulation
- Slow rhythmic rocking (calming)
- Gravity change (controlled movements like head hanging/somersaults)

Environmental modification
- Calming corner (dim light, soft area, headphones)
- Visual/auditory simplification (turning off background TV noise)

III) Family Involvement in Special Education Sessions
[Observing the session/taking notes] → [Live practice with the expert] → [Integration into the home routine] → [Feedback with video]

Recommendations (summary)
- Taking notes on techniques instead of just watching the session.
- In the final part, the parent working with practical coaching.
- Embedding teaching into daily routines with NET (Natural Environment Teaching).
- Establishing a feedback loop with short videos.
